own_scenes.desc: El club legendario que abrieron George Baker y Alton Miller en el centro en el verano de 1988: Miller y Chez Damier pinchaban los sábados para un público sobre todo gay y Darrell «D» Wynn con Derrick May los viernes (May tocó gratis un año entero). Volvió a reunir a la clientela de los preps y a la bohemia negra de Detroit, con la cabina a un piso de altura, el bombo en el pecho, casi sin luces y baile hasta las seis. Detroit no estaba lista para sostenerlo y cerró el 24 de noviembre de 1989, con May mezclando campanadas con «Strings of Life». Llegaba gente de Atlanta, Nueva York y Chicago, y visitas como Depeche Mode o ABC; Matt Cogger aprendió allí y grabó luego como Neuropolitique. «Murió joven y famoso, como el Titanic».

refs.q: I played there for a year for nothing; I never got paid, not a dime, for one year.
refs.para: It was funny, because I had picked that building out about five years before George even saw it, and I said this would be the perfect building for a club. Then George went and got the building. . . . I couldn’t believe it! From there it all came together . . . we all contributed. I played there for a year for nothing; I never got paid, not a dime, for one year. The institute was a tribute to all that we put our hearts and souls into. It was a blessing.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: Time to Express: Techno’s First Artists Emerge, 1981–1989

refs.q: A lot of clubs have been around longer and have had much more prosperous “careers” . . . but the Music Institute is one of those places that died young and famous. It’s like the Titanic—it just lives.
refs.para: It was unbelievable, because it [techno] was new . . . and people [had] never heard it before. We had people driving in from Atlanta . . . New York, Chicago, just to come to the parties. Entertainers would come down to see the club and what it was all about, because it was something special. And I think that’s why it lives on [symbolically] today. A lot of clubs have been around longer and have had much more prosperous “careers” . . . but the Music Institute is one of those places that died young and famous. It’s like the Titanic—it just lives.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: Time to Express: Techno’s First Artists Emerge, 1981–1989
